skill.name: lifi-stablecoin-swap
skill.description: Build LI.FI Intents integrations for 1:1 stablecoin transfers across supported EVM chains. Covers onboarding, quoting, approvals, escrow orders, settlement tracking, and REST alternatives.
skill.summary: Guide LI.FI Intents integrations from stablecoin quote through escrow settlement.
skill.author: internet-court

security_audit.summary: Most static alerts are false positives caused by Markdown backticks, TypeScript templates, relative imports, documentation links, and environment-file labels. Intentional LI.FI API requests and environment-variable reads are confirmed low-risk capabilities. The quickstart also lacks source-chain enforcement, exposes an integrator key to clients, and stops polling before settlement.

remediation.issue: Transactions do not enforce the configured source chain.
remediation.suggestion: Require chain 8453 before allowance checks, approvals, and order opening. Reject or switch networks before requesting any signature.

remediation.issue: The quickstart exposes the integrator key through a public client variable.
remediation.suggestion: Keep the key server-side unless LI.FI explicitly permits public use. Proxy requests and apply authentication, rate limits, and monitoring.

remediation.issue: The status timer stops at Delivered instead of continuing to Settled.
remediation.suggestion: Continue polling until Settled or Expired when settlement finality matters. Present Delivered as an intermediate state.

semantic_findings.title: Missing Source-Chain Enforcement
semantic_findings.description: The examples fix the source asset to Base. Transaction writes use wallet.chain without confirming chain 8453, risking unintended cross-network contract interactions.
semantic_findings.confidence_reasoning: The source chain and token constants are fixed, while transaction writes use wallet.chain. No chain guard or network switch appears in either flow.

semantic_findings.title: Client-Exposed Integrator Key
semantic_findings.description: The quickstart stores the integrator key in NEXT_PUBLIC_LIFI_INTEGRATOR_KEY and reads it from client-side swap code. Browser users can extract and reuse the value.
semantic_findings.confidence_reasoning: The NEXT_PUBLIC prefix makes the value browser-visible in this Next.js client flow. The files do not define whether LI.FI treats the key as secret.

semantic_findings.title: Polling Stops Before Settlement
semantic_findings.description: The quickstart clears polling when status becomes Delivered, although Settled is a later terminal state. Applications may report incomplete settlement finality.
semantic_findings.confidence_reasoning: The status table distinguishes Delivered from Settled, but the timer stops on Delivered. The shown interface therefore cannot continue polling to Settled.

content.value_statement: Stablecoin transfers can lose value through fees, spreads, and cross-chain complexity. This skill guides LI.FI Intents integration for quoted output, escrow execution, and settlement tracking.
actual_capabilities: Explain LI.FI integrator onboarding and 1:1 quote requirements.
Generate TypeScript quote flows with @lifi/intent and bigint amounts.
Build escrow orders and ERC-20 approval steps with viem.
Track orders through Signed, Delivered, Settled, or Expired states.
Provide a Next.js and wagmi quickstart for wallet-connected swaps.
Outline REST quote and order structures for non-TypeScript services.
limitations: Requires a LI.FI integrator account with 1:1 quoting enabled.
Does not verify live chain, route, token, or contract availability.
Example code needs production validation, error handling, network switching, and security review.
Does not provide custody, compliance, tax, or financial advice.

output_examples.input: Explain the integration flow to a payments engineer.
output: Prerequisite: enable 1:1 quoting for the LI.FI integrator.
Flow: request a quote, verify output, approve escrow, open the order, then track settlement.
Receipt: retain source, destination, and order identifiers for reconciliation.
Quote screen with amount, source chain, destination chain, and returned output.
Transaction screen that verifies Base, checks allowance, requests approval, and opens escrow.
Status screen showing Signed, Delivered, Settled, Expired, and transaction links.
Keep integrator credentials according to LI.FI guidance.
Require the expected wallet chain before every signature.
Validate quote expiry, token addresses, amounts, API responses, and terminal order states.
Add timeouts, retries, monitoring, refunds, and user-facing recovery paths.

best_practices: Verify source chain, token addresses, quote expiry, amount, and recipient before every signature.
Keep integrator credentials server-side unless provider documentation explicitly permits client exposure.
Surface order and transaction identifiers for support, reconciliation, and compliance review.
anti_patterns: Do not assume every route or pair supports 1:1 output.
Do not submit approvals or escrow transactions without checking the connected chain.
Do not treat Delivered as final settlement when your workflow requires Settled.

faq.question: Does this skill guarantee 1:1 output?
faq.answer: Only supported pairs and enabled LI.FI integrators receive 1:1 quotes. Always inspect the returned amount before requesting a signature.

faq.question: Which chains and stablecoins are supported?
faq.answer: Coverage changes with solver availability. Query the supported-chain and route endpoints instead of relying on hardcoded lists.

faq.question: Is the TypeScript SDK required?
faq.answer: No. The skill also outlines REST quote requests and escrow order construction for other languages.

faq.question: Does the user pay gas?
faq.answer: Solvers handle destination delivery costs. Source-chain approval and escrow opening can still require wallet transactions.

faq.question: Should the integrator key be public?
faq.answer: Treat it as sensitive unless LI.FI explicitly confirms public use. Avoid NEXT_PUBLIC and proxy requests when secrecy is required.

faq.question: Can the quickstart run unchanged in production?
faq.answer: No. Add chain enforcement, validation, secure credential handling, retries, monitoring, accessibility, and recovery paths before production use.
